content:
#1 While 1D quark strings/gluon flux tubes are considered inside mesons/baryons like in nice Urs Schreiber image in x.com/UrsSchreiber/status/2049890763454976406, there is looking completely neglected question if they could be also formed between nucleons, helping with nuclear binding?

For example en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Halo_nucleus like Li-11 binds 1-2 protons or neutrons in distance much larger than of nuclear force for milliseconds, with 3-body borromean forces - could it be done by some 1D structures: quark strings, topological vortices?

Or en.wikipedia.org/wiki/EMC_effect shows that viewing nucleons as built of 3 quarks no longer works for larger nuclei - suggesting some e.g. quark rearrangement. Already for deuteron - naively p+n has no electric quadrupole moment, but experiments show it is quite large (0.2859 e fm^2) - does it mean some deformation of p+n quark configuration?

There are liquid crystal analogs of nuclei as literally knots of such 1D structures e.g. nature.com/articles/s41567-025-03107-0 - are there any arguments for or against it? The best argument seems string hadronization: assumption used for LHC simulations that in collision there is formed quark string, and it decays into particles - suggesting to search for correspondence, e.g. there can be created various size nuclei, and 1D structures could form various size knots …
subject: Do quark strings/gluon flux tubes help with nuclear binding?

content:
#2 As you may know, a remarkably good, and continuously improving, model for nuclei is as Skyrmions (topologically nontrivial configurations of the meson fields).

This model is not yet close to resolving the subtleties that you mention, but it gives a decent description of nuclei at least up to carbon, which is remarkable enough.

While there have been and remain discrepancies in predicted masses, these have systematically been shrinking the more of the tower of vector mesons is adjoined to the pion field, suggesting that this model is quite on the right track.
subject: Do quark strings/gluon flux tubes help with nuclear binding?

content:
#3 Indeed Skyrmion model is great, but misses EM - e.g. proton and neutron are basically the same. Also I have asked them about halo nuclei, but it is hopeless there - needs quite stable binding in very long distance … like with topological vortices used to model quark strings, which are missing in Skyrmion models. I attend their conference in Kraków for a decade, and recently there is stagnation, people are leaving.

So it needs some modification, new ideas … brought e.g. by liquid crystal experiments - getting e.g. ~Coulomb for quantized topological charges (www.nature.com/articles/s41598-017-16200-z), or mentioned nuclei as knots of topological vortices for quark strings: nature.com/articles/s41567-025-03107-0.

One difference is interpretation of topological charges - Skyrmion people see it as baryon number, e.g. liquid crystal approaches as elementary electric charge. Second is potential - Skyrmion people use with trivial minimum getting only short-range interactions, for long-range we need Higgs-like.

To formalize it, Manfried Faber proposed to interpret curvature of deeper field as dual F tensor - this way Gauss law counts topological charge, getting EM with built-in charge quantization, and regularization of singularities leading to running coupling correction of Coulomb in very low distance/high energy: mdpi.com/2218-1997/11/4/113. Then liquid crystal people mainly use Landau-de Gennes model (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Landau%E2%80%93de_Gennes_theory) missing Lorentz invariance - we can get replacing kinetic term to Skyrme/Faber, improving agreement also getting such nuclei as knots: arXiv:2108.07896
